_comment: Gold Layer Shorts. One entry per clip; files live in assets/shorts/<file>.mp4 and assets/shorts/posters/<file>.jpg. "post" names the slug of the article behind a short, if there is one: the short then appears inside that article. "summary" is the text version of the clip. "youtube" is the YouTube id; from "youtubeFrom" on, the short plays on YouTube (click-to-load) instead of our MP4. "showFrom" (optional) hides a short until that time, e.g. while its YouTube upload is scheduled.

shorts.title: Welcome to Gold Layer City: an anime opening made with AI
shorts.summary: An anime opening for Gold Layer: a night city built from code, three characters and a theme tune made on my own PC. Prof explains why, Nova learns by trying, Kit makes it work. Directed in chat; the AI wrote the city, the cameras, the credits and the motion. No narration: music only, AI-generated.

shorts.title: Power BI layout: headline number top-left
shorts.summary: A report page with the detail on top and the total at the bottom: reading starts top-left, so the total comes last. Move it top-left: big number first, detail follows. Microsoft Learn: "Put the highest level of data at the top left corner and show more detail as you move in the direction the audience uses for reading (left-to-right, top-to-bottom)." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI alt text on every visual with meaning
shorts.summary: Without looking at the chart, a screen reader gets the title, the visual type, then nothing. Add alt text in Format → General → Alt text (limit: 250 characters) and the chart gets described. The strip in the short is an illustration, not a real screen reader's exact words. Microsoft Learn: "Ensure alt text is added to all non-decorative visuals on the page." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI data labels: the squint test
shorts.summary: A chart with a label on every point. Blur it, and the labels win over the trend. Cut the labels you don't need and keep the one that matters. Microsoft Learn: "Avoid cluttering your charts with data labels that aren't needed." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Avoid red + green in Power BI
shorts.summary: Green for met, red for missed. Under a simulated colour-blind lens they look almost the same. The fix in the short: blue and orange, plus an icon and a word in every cell (our choice of pair; Learn names none). Microsoft Learn: "Certain color combinations can be difficult for users to distinguish. These combinations include the following: green and red... Avoid using these colors together in a chart or on the same report page." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI titles: avoid acronyms and jargon
shorts.summary: Visual titles only insiders can read: CY Totals, YTD Rev LC, AOV MTD. Spelled out, they say what each visual shows. CY Totals to Current Year Sales Amount USD Totals is Learn's own example. Microsoft Learn: "Avoid using acronyms or jargon in your report titles." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI text contrast: at least 4.5 to 1
shorts.summary: Pale grey text (#ABABAB) on a white page: a contrast of only 2.3 to 1. Darken the text until it passes 4.5 to 1. Microsoft Learn: "Ensure color contrast between title, axis label, and data label text and the background are at least 4.5:1." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI secondary axis: fix the flat line
shorts.summary: Revenue (millions) and Orders (thousands) on one axis: Orders looks flat all year. As a line and clustered column chart with the secondary y-axis on, Orders shows its real shape. Microsoft Learn: "Try to avoid mixing large and small measures on the same scale... If you need to mix, choose a visualization like a combo chart that allows the use of a second axis." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI: sort every visual on purpose
shorts.summary: A bar chart sorted A to Z: the eye has to hunt. Sort by the measure and the biggest is answered at a glance. Looking up one name in a long list? Then sort by the axis. Microsoft Learn: "Pay attention to how charts are sorted. If you want to draw attention to the highest or lowest number, sort by the measure." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Consistent Power BI charts: colour, order, scale
shorts.summary: Two charts on one page where colour, order and scale don't match. Match colour, order, then scale, and it shows: West halved, $6.0M to $3.0M. Microsoft Learn: "Be consistent with chart scales on axes, chart dimension ordering, and the colors used for dimension values within charts." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Pie charts: fewer than eight categories
shorts.summary: A pie with twelve slices: which product sells most? The slices become sorted bars and the answer is clear. Or keep the pie: top 5 + Other. Microsoft Learn: "Pie charts are best if they have fewer than eight categories." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI tooltips: don't hide key facts
shorts.summary: The answer (North missed target by 12%) hides in a tooltip. Without a mouse it is hard to reach. The fix in the short: the fact goes on the chart, the extras stay in the tooltip. Microsoft Learn: "Don't use tooltips to convey important information." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI: don't rely on colour alone
shorts.summary: Two lines told apart only by colour. In a simulated colour-blind view they look the same. The fix: markers, a dashed line and direct labels, in blue and gold. Microsoft Learn: "Avoid using color... as the only way of conveying information. Instead, use markers to convey different series." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI: be careful with axes not at zero
shorts.summary: On-time delivery, 97.0% vs 98.5%, on an axis that starts at 96%: it looks like a huge jump. From zero, the same data shows a 1.5 point gap. Microsoft Learn: "Be careful when you use charts that distort reality, such as 3-D charts and charts that don't start at zero." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: Power BI: show 3.4M, not 3,400,000
shorts.summary: A report with every number in full (3,412,876). Cards on Display units Auto with one decimal read 3.4M and 48.2K; data labels on Millions with one decimal read 1.3M. Microsoft Learn: "Don't exceed three or four numerals when displaying numbers... use 3.4 million instead of 3,400,000." Same rule whether a person or an AI agent built the report.

shorts.title: 14 tests, 2 days: what broke making an AI anime teacher
shorts.summary: We tried giving our videos anime characters, starting with a teacher for a quiz short. The AI wrote every line of motion code. Each mistake next to its fix: a hologram that just stood there, stand-in school uniforms, the same wave every line, bikes that weren't bikes. And one thing that's still broken: the hair goes through the arm. Narrated by an AI voice.

shorts.title: Every visual is its own file: the report folder
shorts.summary: Save a Power BI report as a project (PBIP) and the report becomes a folder of JSON files in PBIR: one folder per page, one per visual, a file per bookmark, and your themes in StaticResources. Watch out: filter values like 'Contoso' can land in visual.json.

shorts.title: One table, one file: the semantic model folder
shorts.summary: Save a Power BI report as a project (PBIP) and the semantic model becomes a folder of text files in TMDL: one file per table, plus relationships, expressions, roles and the settings. Two files never go in Git: .pbi/localSettings.json (just you) and .pbi/cache.abf (your data).

shorts.title: Pareto chart in Power BI in 4 steps
shorts.summary: Sort the bars biggest first, add the cumulative %, draw the 80% cutoff and read the vital few. On Contoso sample data, 4 of 8 product categories make 83% of revenue. In Power BI the cumulative % is one visual calculation: RUNNINGSUM ( [Percent of grand total], ORDERBY ( [Revenue], DESC ) ).

shorts.title: Which PBIP files can your AI agent touch?
shorts.summary: Hand an AI agent the definition/ folders: PBIR for the report, TMDL for the model. Keep it away from .pbi/cache.abf (your data) and .pbi/localSettings.json (just you), and leave mobileState.json and diagramLayout.json alone: no edits outside Desktop. Validate PBIR against its schemas; filter values can still sit in the report files.

shorts.title: The data hiding in your report files
shorts.summary: A .pbix carries your imported data inside it. Save as PBIP and the definition becomes plain text, but the data sits in .pbi/cache.abf. Keep it out of Git with .gitignore, and check visual.json: filter values can still land there.
